strengths: The core idea—injecting self-supervised DINO features as higher-level scene supervision into dense neural SLAM—is sensible, well-motivated, and clearly distinguished from semantic SLAM (no annotations or predefined categories required).

Strong evidence of generality: Table 4 shows consistent improvements when the proposed SSE is plugged into four different scene-encoding backbones (hash-grid, tri-planes, neural points, 3DGS) as well as a method already using semantic cues (SNI-SLAM). This controlled 'baseline vs. +DINO' comparison is the most convincing part of the paper and directly supports the claim that the contribution is a general design strategy rather than a system-specific trick.

Evaluation spans three standard benchmarks (Replica, ScanNet, TUM) covering reconstruction, rendering (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS), and tracking (ATE RMSE), with both neural implicit and explicit pipelines; results are competitive or state-of-the-art within their respective method families.

Component ablation (Table 5) reasonably separates the contribution of raw DINO features, the enriched EDINO features, and the global BA module, supporting the claim that the SSE's structural enrichment matters beyond raw DINO supervision.
Performance/memory analysis (Table 6) is a welcome addition, showing the added features do not incur disproportionate cost relative to strong baselines.
Appropriate attribution: the paper is transparent that the pipelines build on ESLAM, MonoGS, etc., and clearly positions the contribution as orthogonal, plug-in scene-structure enrichment.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is moderate: DINO/feature-level supervision of neural maps is an incremental step over existing color/depth-supervised SLAM, and the SSE itself is a fairly lightweight two-stage cross-attention + MLP design whose benefit over simpler fusion strategies (e.g., concatenation, single attention) is not ablated—Table 5 only compares 'with vs. without' features, not SSE design choices.

Several methodological details are underspecified or ambiguous, hurting reproducibility and clarity: Eq. (7) supervises tri-planes τd with 2D EDINO feature maps f_ed without explaining how a 3D tri-plane and a 2D feature map are compared; Eq. (10) presents a 'modified Gaussian' that does not actually show where the per-Gaussian EDINO feature f_ed^i enters; and how f_ed^i is 'assigned into the distinct channel of Gaussian parameters' is vague. No code release is mentioned, which compounds the reproducibility concern.

Gains over the strongest baselines are often modest (e.g., TUM average ATE 1.36 vs. MonoGS 1.47; ScanNet NeRF 7.1 vs. ESLAM 7.4, and PLGSLAM at 6.8 remains better), so the 'state-of-the-art' framing in the abstract overstates the margin in some cases; the paper is honest about PLGSLAM in Sec. 4.1 but not in the abstract.

Evaluation is limited to indoor RGB-D benchmarks; robustness in the conditions the introduction motivates (poor texture, challenging lighting, dynamic content) is not directly tested, and only 3 TUM sequences are used for tracking claims. There is no limitations discussion or societal-impact statement.

Some internal inconsistencies and sloppiness reduce confidence: Table 1 lists SplaTAM PSNR 33.97 while Table 4 lists 34.11 for the same method; loss weights are reported inconsistently (DINO loss 1 in Sec. 4 for 3DGS, 0.01 for NeRF's DINO loss with 5.0 encoding loss) without justification; minor typos ('componentes', unclosed parenthesis).

The framing as 'two foundational paradigms' inflates what are essentially engineering integrations of an existing feature extractor into two existing SLAM frameworks; the contribution type is closer to Applied/Systems than a new algorithmic paradigm, which slightly tempers the significance assessment.

strengths: Broad empirical coverage: the proposed design is evaluated across two paradigms (NeRF-based and 3DGS-based SLAM) and three standard benchmarks (Replica, ScanNet, TUM), with comparisons to a reasonable set of recent baselines.

The generality ablation (Table 4) is the most convincing part of the paper: augmenting several existing SLAM systems (Co-SLAM, ESLAM, Point-SLAM, SplaTAM, MonoGS, SNI-SLAM) with the proposed features yields consistent, if modest, improvements, suggesting the idea is architecture-agnostic.
A dedicated runtime/memory analysis (Table 6) and component-level ablations (Table 5) are provided, and the systems remain competitive in speed and footprint.
The manuscript is generally well organized and clearly written, with the pipelines described at a level of detail sufficient to understand the design.
weaknesses: The central conceptual claim — that the Scene Structure Encoder (SSE) captures 'hierarchical scene elements and their structural relationships' — is never substantiated. All evaluation is limited to geometric/rendering/tracking metrics; there is no probing, semantic, or downstream-understanding analysis of the EDINO features. As written, EDINO is functionally just another supervised feature map, and the paper's framing oversells what the evidence shows.

The novelty is limited and prior art is not adequately attributed. Feature-based (including DINO/LSeg-style) supervision in neural and 3DGS SLAM has been explored before, yet the related work asserts that existing methods 'overlook the potential of the standalone DINO features'. The method itself is largely standard: MLP encodings plus two cross-attention layers, then L1 feature distillation losses added to existing SLAM frameworks.

The ablation undermines the core contribution: adding raw DINO features alone (rows B and D in Table 5) already recovers most of the gain over the baseline, and the SSE/EDINO component adds only a marginal further improvement. The scientific case for the SSE as the key contribution is therefore weak.

Reported gains are incremental and often not state of the art despite the abstract's claim: on Replica the NeRF variant is worse than Point-SLAM in accuracy (1.94 vs 1.41) and depth L1 (0.66 vs 0.44); on ScanNet the NeRF variant trails PLGSLAM by a clear margin (7.1 vs 6.8 ATE). The claim of 'superior performance' is selective.

Several technical details are unclear or questionable. In particular, Eq. (7) imposes an L1 loss directly between a tri-plane representation τd and a 2D EDINO feature map f_ed, with no explanation of the dimensional correspondence or how this supervision is applied spatially.

Evaluation consistency is a concern: Table 4 states that metrics for baselines and DINO-extended variants are 'as reported in the original papers', mixing evaluations with potentially different protocols; some numbers also appear inconsistent with Table 1 (e.g., SplaTAM PSNR 33.97 vs 34.11). The comparison against SNI-SLAM uses a baseline that relies on ground-truth semantic masks, which complicates interpretation.

Benchmark scope is narrow for a systems claim: TUM uses only 3 sequences, ScanNet reconstruction is not evaluated for the NeRF variant, and no dynamic or outdoor scenes are tested. There is no mention of code release, limiting reproducibility.

No limitations discussion is provided; future work mentions loop-closure and sub-mapping, implicitly acknowledging that the current system lacks these standard SLAM capabilities, but this is not reflected in the claims.

strengths: The core idea of injecting self-supervised DINO features (and a learned enrichment of them, EDINO) into dense SLAM as an additional supervisory signal is sensible and, within the NeRF/3DGS-SLAM literature, relatively unexplored; it avoids the annotations and predefined categories required by semantic SLAM.

The generality of the proposal is convincingly demonstrated: the SSE module is grafted onto hash-grid (Co-SLAM), tri-plane (ESLAM, SNI-SLAM), neural-point (Point-SLAM), and 3DGS (SplaTAM, MonoGS) backbones, with consistent (if modest) improvements in all cases (Table 4), which supports the claim that the contribution is orthogonal to the underlying scene representation.

Evaluation is reasonably extensive: three standard benchmarks (Replica, ScanNet, TUM), both an implicit and an explicit pipeline, tracking/mapping/rendering metrics, component and generality ablations, plus a memory/runtime analysis (Table 6) showing favorable footprint compared to Point-SLAM, SNI-SLAM, SplaTAM, etc.

The 3DGS-based variant shows genuinely strong tracking results on the harder real-world data (ScanNet avg. 9.5 cm vs. 11.9 cm for SplaTAM; TUM avg. 1.36 cm), and the NeRF variant improves completion/completion-rate on Replica.
The paper is generally well written and organized, with clear figures illustrating both pipelines and the loss structure.
weaknesses: Technical clarity of the SSE is insufficient. Equations (2)-(3) read as cross-attention with somewhat ad-hoc key/value/query assignments (softmax(fg fa^T) applied to fd, then fg f_atten-d^T applied to fa), but the paper never explains how this yields 'hierarchical scene elements and structural relationships' beyond the naming. Moreover, the training procedure for the SSE (MLPs Fed, Feg, Fea and attention modules) is never specified: it is unclear whether SSE is trained end-to-end through the SLAM losses or with a separate objective; since DINO is frozen and EDINO only supervises the tri-plane (Eq. 7), the actual learning signal is ambiguous. Similarly, Eq. (7) compares the tri-plane τd directly with EDINO features, leaving the dimensionality correspondence unexplained.

The component ablation (Table 5, lower) partially contradicts the narrative. For the 3DGS pipeline on ScanNet, removing DINO features entirely (C) changes PSNR from 21.43 to 21.50, SSIM/LPIPS are essentially identical, and depth L1 improves from 0.49 to 0.47; only ATE RMSE (12.67 vs 9.55) shows a meaningful gain. Yet the text claims 'substantial performance degradation across mapping, rendering, and tracking metrics'. The evidence mainly supports a tracking benefit, not a rendering/mapping one.

The 'state-of-the-art' claim is overstated. On Replica reconstruction, Point-SLAM retains better accuracy (1.41 vs 1.94) and depth L1 (0.44 vs 0.66); on ScanNet tracking PLGSLAM is better (6.8 vs 7.1); on TUM the NeRF variant essentially matches ESLAM. The gains over the strongest baselines are consistently small and the paper should temper its claims accordingly.

Comparison protocol concerns: Table 4 states that metrics are 'reported in the original papers', mixing evaluation protocols across rows; the SNI-SLAM baseline uses ground-truth semantic masks, making its '+DINO' comparison of limited evidential value. Several 3DGS baselines also differ from Table 1 values (e.g., SplaTAM PSNR 33.97 vs 34.11) without explanation.

The mechanism by which DINO supervision improves tracking is not analyzed: tracking explicitly optimizes only color/depth residuals (Sec. 3.3), so the large ATE improvements attributed to DINO cues in Table 5 lack a convincing explanation. A qualitative analysis of what the EDINO features encode (e.g., PCA visualizations) would substantially strengthen the paper's central claim about 'scene understanding'.

No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility for a system paper whose gains are incremental; neither is there a discussion of limitations (synthetic-heavy evaluation, indoor RGB-D only, no loop closure, non-real-time at 0.61-2.55 FPS).

Novelty positioning could be sharper: distilling ViT/DINO features into NeRF/3DGS representations is well established outside SLAM (e.g., semantic/feature-field distillation works), so the paper should more carefully delineate what is new relative to that line of work rather than claiming both implicit and explicit methods 'overlook' standalone DINO features.

strengths: The core idea — lifting DINOv2 features with depth-based geometry awareness via a Scene Geometry Encoder (SGE) before injecting them into SLAM scene representations — is sensible, clearly motivated, and addresses a real gap: prior feature-informed SLAM systems either ignore foundation-model features or use them without 3D structure.

Generality is convincingly demonstrated: the SGE is integrated into seven heterogeneous systems (hash-grids, tri-planes, neural points, 3D Gaussians, 2D surfels), with consistent improvements across all of them (Table 1), which supports the plug-and-play claim better than a single-system evaluation would.

The component ablation (Table 2) directly tests the paper's central claim: vanilla DINO gives marginal gains, simple depth concatenation (B') partially helps, and geoDINO roughly doubles the improvement — a well-designed control experiment.

Evaluation is broad: three standard benchmarks (Replica, ScanNet, TUM), reconstruction, rendering, and tracking metrics, plus robustness to depth noise (Table 4) and a thorough computational breakdown (Tables 7-8) showing moderate overhead.
Multiple prior works already use DINO/DINOv2 in SLAM are properly discussed and differentiated (Section 2), giving fair attribution.
Depth-noise robustness experiment is a thoughtful addition given the method's reliance on depth.
weaknesses: Technical soundness of key formulations is underspecified. Eq. (6) defines L_gf = ||τ_D − f_gD||_1, but τ_D is a tri-plane (3D latent volume) while f_gD is a per-pixel feature map — how these are aligned in space and dimensionality is never explained, leaving the most important loss of the NeRF pipeline unclear. Similarly, the GS pipeline's mechanism for assigning geoDINO embeddings to Gaussians (fusing into 'parameters' as in Fig. 5) and how f'_gD is obtained during splatting lacks detail; Eq. (11) renders f'_D but the text claims geoDINO is inserted, blurring which features are supervised versus rendered.

The SGE is claimed to be 'optimized online,' yet the supervision signals for its own training (what supervises f_gD, beyond its use as a loss target for τ_D?) and the training curriculum are not described, raising questions about what actually gets learned versus whether geometry injection alone suffices.

Gains are uneven across benchmarks and somewhat synthetic-data-heavy: the largest improvements (e.g., Depth L1 0.43→0.12, PSNR +1.2 on GauS-SLAM) are on Replica, while on the real ScanNet the NeRF variant does not clearly beat its own baseline on scene 0000 and PLGSLAM remains better; on TUM, MonoGS, SEGS-SLAM and VSS-SLAM beat DINO-SLAM on individual sequences. Only average values lead.
The NeRF variant roughly halves FPS relative to ESLAM (4.62→2.55), a non-trivial cost that is acknowledged but not analyzed; the practical trade-off for real-time use deserves discussion.

Methodological novelty is moderate: cross-attention fusion of two projected feature streams (Eqs. 2-3) is a standard mechanism; the contribution is primarily a design/empirical one rather than a new algorithmic idea, and the writing occasionally overstates it ('foundational paradigms').
No loop closure or sub-mapping, so applicability is limited to small indoor trajectories, as the authors concede only briefly in the conclusion; societal impact and limitations discussion is minimal.

No explicit code release or project page content is provided (the 'Project page:' line on page 1 is empty), limiting reproducibility given the many implementation details needed (feature fusion dimensions, Gaussian channel assignment, resolution schedules).

strengths: The proposed SGE/geoDINO idea is evaluated for breadth of applicability: the authors integrate their module into seven different SLAM backbones (hash grids, tri-planes, neural points, 3D Gaussians, 2D surfels), which is a more thorough generality study than typical incremental SLAM papers.

The ablation in Table 2 is well designed for the core claim: it separates vanilla DINO, simple depth concatenation (B'), and the proposed geoDINO (C), providing evidence that the gains come from geometry-aware lifting rather than from merely adding features.

Comprehensive evaluation on three standard benchmarks (Replica, ScanNet, TUM), plus useful practical analyses: runtime/memory breakdown (Table 8), FPS overhead across backbones, and a depth-noise robustness experiment (Table 4).

The writing and figure-based overview of the two pipelines (implicit vs. explicit) is generally clear, and the method is implemented as an add-on with modest overhead, which increases practical relevance.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The SGE is a fairly standard attention-based fusion of frozen DINOv2 features with depth-derived features, and the supervision is plain L1 feature-matching losses. Given that DINO features are already used in SLAM [28,37,40,56,61,62], the conceptual delta is incremental, and the paper's framing as two 'foundational paradigms' overstates the contribution.

Overclaiming and inconsistency between the teaser and the results. Fig. 1 claims 'superior camera tracking accuracy' (Ours 6.2cm vs SOTA 7.0cm), yet Table 5 shows the NeRF variant averages 6.9 ATE on ScanNet, slightly worse than PLGSLAM (6.8), and the PSNR values displayed in the teaser (Ours 44.19 vs SOTA 44.6) actually show the method behind SOTA. The reported numbers in Fig. 1 do not match the tables, which undermines confidence.

The central mechanism is under-analyzed. The paper asserts that vanilla DINO 'lacks 3D geometry understanding,' but provides no analysis (visualizations, probing, or feature similarity studies) of what geoDINO features encode or why feature-level L1 supervision improves camera tracking. The improvement in pose accuracy from adding semantic/feature losses is plausible but not explained.

Unclear formulation of the geoDINO tri-plane loss (Eq. 6). L_gf = ||τ_D − f_gD||_1 supervises a 3D tri-plane representation with per-frame 2D feature maps; how these quantities are aligned dimensionally and spatially (projection, sampling, back-projection) is not described, leaving a key component of the method underspecified and hard to reproduce.

No downstream semantic evaluation despite the motivation. The paper motivates the work by 'higher-level scene understanding' and semantic comprehension, but reports only geometric/rendering/tracking metrics; there is no segmentation or open-vocabulary task showing that the injected features actually carry usable semantics.

Evaluation breadth issues: TUM uses only three sequences; ScanNet NeRF results trail a tailored baseline; and most reconstruction gains are reported on the synthetic Replica dataset where depth is near-perfect, which is precisely the condition the SGE depends on. The depth-noise experiment is a good start but limited to one scene and one noise level.

Reproducibility is weak: the 'Project page' link is a placeholder, no code release is stated, several design details (SGE capacity, how features are attached to Gaussians, BA details) are underspecified, and the geoDINO loss formulation is ambiguous.

Presentation issues: the joint-authorship marker is orphaned, author block is missing/incomplete, and minor notation/typographical problems (e.g., inconsistent naming GauS-SLAM, Eq. 5 formatting) suggest the manuscript was not carefully polished.

strengths: The core idea is clearly motivated: vanilla DINO features lack 3D geometric awareness, and the proposed Scene Geometry Encoder (SGE) lifts DINO features with depth cues via a cross-attention mechanism, which is a simple but sensible design.

The generality of the approach is convincingly demonstrated: the SGE is integrated into five different scene representations (hash-grids, tri-planes, neural points, 3D Gaussians, 2D Gaussian surfels) built on multiple SLAM backbones (Table 1), consistently improving performance across the board, including over systems that already use DINO features (SNI-SLAM).

The ablation study (Table 2) directly supports the central claim: vanilla DINO yields only marginal gains, concatenating depth features helps slightly, while geoDINO roughly doubles the improvement on most metrics, ruling out the trivial alternative of simply concatenating depth.
Strong empirical results: state-of-the-art or near-SOTA performance on Replica (both NeRF and GS variants), competitive tracking on ScanNet, and best average ATE on TUM across three sequences.

Good experimental hygiene: runtime and memory breakdowns (Tables 7-8) quantify the overhead of SGE, a depth-noise robustness study (Table 4) addresses an obvious concern about relying on depth, and the paper is generally well organized and clearly written.
The design is plug-and-play and orthogonal to the underlying SLAM architecture, which increases its potential impact on future NeRF/GS-based SLAM systems.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is moderate: the SGE is essentially a two-stage cross-attention module injecting depth-derived features into DINO embeddings. The claim of 'two foundational paradigms' feels overstated, as both pipelines largely follow existing SLAM frameworks (ESLAM, GauS-SLAM) with an additional feature loss; the main contribution is the feature enhancement strategy rather than a new SLAM architecture.

Several methodological details are underspecified, hurting reproducibility: how exactly the tri-plane encoding tau_D is compared with the 2D geoDINO feature map in Eq. (6) (dimensions and sampling procedure), how a single geoDINO feature is associated with each Gaussian in the GS pipeline, and how SGE behaves at inference/tracking time are not clearly explained.

Some comparisons rely on numbers 'reported in the original papers' rather than re-running baselines under a unified protocol, which raises questions about strict comparability (e.g., evaluation scripts, mesh post-processing, sequence subsets).

The NeRF variant is not clearly SOTA on ScanNet (PLGSLAM performs better) and the GS variant is behind MonoGS/VSS-SLAM on individual TUM sequences; the paper acknowledges this, but the breadth of the SOTA claim in the abstract is somewhat stronger than the evidence.

Evaluation is limited to indoor RGB-D benchmarks; generalization to monocular setups, dynamic scenes, or outdoor data is untested, and there is no qualitative analysis of the geoDINO feature maps themselves that would explain *why* geometry-aware lifting helps (beyond aggregate metrics).

Minor presentation issues: a typo in Table 3 ('LPIP'), the roles of keys/queries in Eqs. (2)-(3) are confusingly described (f_g appears as query in one place and key in another), and the project page listed on page 1 appears empty, which weakens reproducibility support.
